subtopic_detail: Initial gait and balance assessment after a single non-syncopal fall
stem:
A 79-year-old woman attends your general practice after catching her foot on a rug at home last week. She landed on her hands and got up without help; she did not hit her head.

She lives alone in a single-storey house and manages her own shopping. Her only regular medicine is perindopril. She describes no light-headedness or blackout around the time of the fall.

Heart sounds are dual and her visual acuity is 6/9 in each eye with her glasses on. She steadies herself on the furniture as she walks across the consulting room. Both knees show crepitus and reduced range of movement.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min regular, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg supine and 136/76 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily, paracetamol 1 g as required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial assessment?

options.text: Arrange a non-contrast CT brain to exclude an intracranial cause of falling
options.rationale: Imaging the brain is not indicated when there was no head strike, no loss of consciousness and no focal neurological sign; it would be appropriate if she were anticoagulated and had struck her head. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls

options.text: Request a 24-hour ambulatory electrocardiogram to look for an intermittent arrhythmia
options.rationale: Rhythm monitoring is reserved for falls with syncope, palpitations or an abnormal resting electrocardiogram; a witnessed trip with no prodrome does not meet that threshold. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls

options.text: Perform a timed up-and-go test with direct observation of her gait
options.rationale: Observed gait and balance testing is the first-line bedside assessment after a fall and takes under a minute; a timed up-and-go beyond 12 seconds identifies the mobility impairment that her furniture-walking already suggests and directs her to a strength and balance programme. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls

options.text: Refer her for bone densitometry before undertaking any further clinical assessment
options.rationale: Densitometry addresses fracture risk, not fall risk, and does not change the immediate assessment; it is worth arranging later but it is not the initial step. (Source: ANZSGM position statement on comprehensive geriatric assessment)
source_refs: ANZSGM position statement on comprehensive geriatric assessment

options.text: Arrange an echocardiogram to assess her for structural valvular heart disease
options.rationale: Echocardiography is driven by an abnormal cardiac examination or syncope, and her heart sounds are normal with no murmur. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls

explanation.summary: About a third of Australians over 65 fall each year, and a fall is a sentinel event that should trigger assessment even when no injury occurs. The initial assessment is clinical and bedside: gait and balance observation, lying and standing blood pressure, vision, footwear, medication review and a check for cognitive impairment. Investigations are added only when the history or examination points to a specific cause, such as syncope or focal neurology. Supervised strength and balance training is the intervention with the strongest evidence for reducing falls in community-dwelling older people. In context, a fall in an older person is a clinical event to be assessed at the bedside first, with investigations reserved for the features that the history and examination actually raise.
key_points: Observed gait and balance testing is the first step after any fall in an older person
A timed up-and-go beyond 12 seconds flags impaired mobility and predicts further falls
Investigations follow the history and examination; they do not replace them
Osteoarthritis and lower limb weakness are common, modifiable contributors to tripping falls
explanation.pearls: A timed up-and-go over 12 seconds identifies an older person who needs a supervised strength and balance programme of at least 50 hours total to reduce fall rates.

sources.label: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls
ANZSGM position statement on comprehensive geriatric assessment

subtopic_detail: Primary prevention of delirium in a high-risk surgical admission
stem:
You are the admitting resident for an 83-year-old woman who has fractured the neck of her right femur after a fall at home. She is booked for hemiarthroplasty tomorrow afternoon.

Her daughter reports that she has been forgetting appointments for the past two years but still manages at home with prompting. She wears glasses and two hearing aids, neither of which came in with the ambulance. She has never had an episode of confusion in hospital before.

On assessment she is orientated to time, place and person, and her abbreviated mental test score is 8 out of 10. She has received one dose of intravenous morphine in the emergency department and reports her hip pain as 3 out of 10 at rest.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86/min, blood pressure 132/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, urea and creatinine all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action to reduce her risk of delirium?

options.text: Start a multicomponent programme addressing orientation, sleep, mobility and sensory aids
options.rationale: Multicomponent non-pharmacological prevention is the only intervention shown to reduce incident delirium, cutting it by around a third in at-risk hospitalised older people; retrieving her glasses and hearing aids is part of that bundle. (Source: ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard)

options.text: Prescribe regular oral haloperidol 0.5 mg twice daily until after her operation
options.rationale: Antipsychotics have no established role in preventing delirium and carry extrapyramidal, cardiac and mortality risk in older people; haloperidol is reserved for severe distress or risk of harm during established delirium. (Source: ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard)

options.text: Prescribe melatonin 2 mg nightly from admission until the day of discharge
options.rationale: Melatonin is sometimes used for sleep-wake disturbance but the prevention evidence is inconsistent and it is not a substitute for the multicomponent programme. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Order a non-contrast CT brain and screen for occult infection before theatre
options.rationale: Investigations look for precipitants of an established delirium; she is currently cognitively intact and there is no clinical pointer to infection or intracranial pathology. (Source: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people)
source_refs: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people

options.text: Restrict her analgesia to paracetamol alone to avoid opioid-induced confusion after theatre
options.rationale: Undertreated pain is itself one of the strongest precipitants of postoperative delirium after hip fracture; the aim is adequate analgesia, ideally opioid-sparing with a regional block, not opioid avoidance. (Source: ACSQHC Hip Fracture Care Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: ACSQHC Hip Fracture Care Clinical Care Standard

explanation.summary: Delirium complicates up to half of hip fracture admissions in older people and is associated with longer stay, functional decline and increased mortality. Prevention is far more effective than treatment, and the evidence base sits with multicomponent programmes that target the modifiable precipitants together: sensory aids, orientation, sleep hygiene, early mobilisation, hydration, bowel and bladder care, and pain control. Pharmacological prophylaxis, including antipsychotics and cholinesterase inhibitors, has not been shown to work. Surgery within 48 hours and regional analgesia both reduce delirium risk in hip fracture. In context, prevention bundles outperform every drug studied for delirium, and their components are cheap, ward-level and available on the day of admission.
key_points: Pre-existing cognitive impairment and sensory impairment are the dominant delirium risk factors
Multicomponent non-pharmacological prevention reduces incident delirium by roughly one third
No drug is recommended for delirium prophylaxis
Untreated pain precipitates delirium; opioid avoidance is not a prevention strategy
explanation.pearls: Getting a patient's own glasses and hearing aids to the bedside within the first 24 hours is one of the highest-yield single actions in delirium prevention, and applies before any drug is considered.

sources.label: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people
ACSQHC Hip Fracture Care Clinical Care Standard

subtopic_detail: Hypoactive presentation misattributed to low mood
stem:
An 81-year-old man is on day 4 of treatment for community-acquired pneumonia. The nursing staff ask you to review him because he has become withdrawn, is eating very little and takes a long time to answer questions. They wonder whether he has become depressed since his wife died last year.

His daughter tells you he was managing his own finances and driving to bowls twice a week until this admission, and that he seemed himself when she visited on the day he came in.

At the bedside he is drowsy and loses the thread mid-sentence, but the nursing notes record him as alert and chatting at 8 am. He denies feeling sad and says he simply feels tired.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 124/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 93% on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 12.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 68 mg/L (<5), sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 92 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start mirtazapine 15 mg at night and review his mood again in two weeks
options.rationale: Starting an antidepressant labels a fluctuating attentional disturbance as depression and adds a sedating drug that will worsen it; mirtazapine would be reasonable only once delirium has been excluded and low mood persists. (Source: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people)
source_refs: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people

options.text: Start regular quetiapine 12.5 mg at night to settle his fluctuating daytime state
options.rationale: Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium and are not indicated for the hypoactive form, where the patient is not distressed or at risk of harm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange an inpatient psychiatry consultation for assessment of a major depressive disorder
options.rationale: Referral defers the assessment that can be done at the bedside now, and psychomotor slowing with fluctuating attention is far more commonly delirium than depression in this setting. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Delirium)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Delirium

options.text: Screen for delirium at the bedside and review his precipitants and medications
options.rationale: Fluctuating attention with an acute change from his baseline in an unwell older inpatient is delirium until proven otherwise; a short validated screen such as the 4AT plus a search for precipitants, including hypoxaemia and newly charted drugs, is the correct immediate step. (Source: ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard)

options.text: Arrange an MRI brain and formal neuropsychological testing before any further treatment
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is reserved for focal signs, head injury or unexplained failure to improve, and formal cognitive testing is invalid while attention fluctuates. (Source: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people)
source_refs: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people

explanation.summary: Hypoactive delirium is the most common form in older inpatients and the most frequently missed, because a quiet, withdrawn patient causes no trouble on the ward. It is routinely misread as depression, fatigue or dementia, and carries a worse prognosis than the hyperactive form. The discriminating features are acuity of onset, fluctuation through the day and inattention, which is why a structured screen at the bedside outperforms clinical impression. Once identified, management is to find and fix precipitants: infection, hypoxaemia, pain, constipation, urinary retention, dehydration and culprit medicines. In context, any acute change in an older inpatient's alertness or engagement deserves a structured attention test before it is given a psychiatric label.
key_points: Inattention plus acute onset and fluctuation defines delirium regardless of psychomotor activity
Hypoactive delirium is commonly mislabelled as depression in older inpatients
A collateral history establishes the cognitive baseline and the time course
Treatment is finding and correcting precipitants, not prescribing a sedative
explanation.pearls: The 4AT takes about two minutes, needs no special training, and a score of 4 or more indicates probable delirium; a score of 1 to 3 suggests cognitive impairment warranting further assessment.

sources.label: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people
RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Delirium

subtopic_detail: Searching for a reversible precipitant before sedating an agitated postoperative patient
stem:
You are the night resident called to an 84-year-old man on day 2 after a hemiarthroplasty for a fractured neck of femur. Since midnight he has been pulling at his intravenous cannula and trying to climb over the bed rails. He was calm and orientated at the evening ward round.

He answers questions in single words and keeps reaching towards his lower abdomen. His indwelling catheter was removed at 10 am and the fluid balance chart records no urine output since.

His analgesia chart shows regular paracetamol only; the oxycodone charted in recovery was ceased when the spinal block wore off.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, blood pressure 156/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 42 mg/L (<5), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give haloperidol 0.5 mg orally now, repeating in two hours if he remains agitated
options.rationale: Sedation without a search for the precipitant treats the observer's problem rather than the patient's, and an antipsychotic will worsen urinary retention through its anticholinergic effect. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Assess him for pain and urinary retention, including a bedside bladder scan
options.rationale: Retention and undertreated pain are the two most common and most rapidly reversible precipitants of postoperative delirium, and both are signposted here by the 14 hours without voiding and the ceased opioid; a bladder scan settles the first within minutes. (Source: ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard)

options.text: Give lorazepam 0.5 mg sublingually and nurse him in a low-stimulus single room
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines prolong and deepen delirium except when it is caused by alcohol or sedative withdrawal, and add to his fall risk on a fresh hip. (Source: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people)
source_refs: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people

options.text: Send a urine culture and start empirical oral trimethoprim for presumed infection
options.rationale: He is afebrile with a normal white cell count and a postoperative C-reactive protein rise, so treating a presumed urinary infection risks anchoring on a positive dipstick that reflects colonisation. (Source: ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard)

options.text: Apply a physical restraint and arrange one-to-one nursing observation through the night
options.rationale: Physical restraint increases injury, delirium duration and mortality; one-to-one observation is a supportive measure but does not address the cause. (Source: ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard)

explanation.summary: Agitation after hip surgery in an older person is delirium until proven otherwise, and the clinical task is to find the precipitant rather than to suppress the behaviour. The highest-yield reversible causes at the bedside are pain, urinary retention, constipation, hypoxaemia, and recently charted or recently ceased drugs. Non-pharmacological measures come first; an antipsychotic is reserved for severe distress or behaviour that puts the patient or others at risk, at the lowest dose for the shortest time. Postoperative inflammatory markers rise predictably and should not be read as evidence of infection. In context, agitation in an older surgical patient is a signal to examine the patient rather than a prescription cue.
key_points: Pain and urinary retention are the two quickest reversible precipitants to exclude
Anticholinergic and sedative drugs both worsen delirium and retention
A positive urine dipstick in an afebrile older inpatient is usually colonisation
Physical restraint worsens outcomes and is not a management step
explanation.pearls: A post-void residual above 300 mL on bedside bladder scan warrants catheterisation, and relieving retention can settle postoperative agitation within the hour without any sedative.

sources.label: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people

subtopic_detail: Palliative emergency with evolving cord signs
stem:
A 68-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer presents to the emergency department with five days of mid-thoracic back pain that is worse when he lies flat and wakes him at night. For the past two days his legs have felt heavy and he has needed both arms to push himself out of a chair.

He takes slow-release morphine 20 mg twice daily, which has not helped the back pain, and abiraterone with prednisolone.

Power is 4 out of 5 for hip flexion on both sides with normal upper limb power. Knee and ankle reflexes are brisk and both plantar responses are extensor. He last passed urine nine hours ago and says his bladder feels full.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 142/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), prostate specific antigen rising over three months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Arrange an urgent CT of the lumbar spine and review it in the morning
options.rationale: CT is insensitive for epidural disease and the wrong region has been chosen given the thoracic pain and upper motor neurone signs; delay of a further night risks irreversible paraplegia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Increase his slow-release morphine and arrange an outpatient MRI within a fortnight
options.rationale: Escalating analgesia alone treats the symptom and ignores an evolving neurological deficit; outpatient timing is far outside the window in which function can be preserved. (Source: Palliative Care Australia)

options.text: Refer directly for urgent radiotherapy planning without further imaging of the spine
options.rationale: Radiotherapy is a definitive treatment here but cannot be planned without imaging to define the level and extent of disease. (Source: eviQ Radiation Oncology: Bone metastases (palliative))

options.text: Request urgent neurosurgical review after plain radiographs of the whole spine today
options.rationale: Plain films miss epidural compression in a substantial minority of cases and a normal film would falsely reassure; surgical review is appropriate but follows the MRI. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Give dexamethasone 16 mg orally now and arrange urgent MRI of the whole spine
options.rationale: High-dose corticosteroid started immediately reduces peritumoural oedema while whole-spine MRI, the definitive investigation, is arranged; whole-spine imaging is required because a third of patients have disease at more than one level. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

explanation.summary: Metastatic epidural spinal cord compression affects around 5 per cent of patients with advanced cancer and is most common in prostate, breast and lung primaries. Back pain that is worse lying flat or at night precedes neurological signs by weeks, and that window is the opportunity to preserve function. Once weakness or sphincter disturbance appears, treatment is measured in hours: corticosteroid immediately, urgent whole-spine MRI, then radiotherapy or surgical decompression depending on stability, prognosis and radiosensitivity. Ambulatory status at the time of treatment is the single strongest predictor of walking afterwards. In context, a new neurological symptom in a patient with bone metastases compresses the timeline from weeks to hours.
key_points: Nocturnal or supine-worse back pain in known malignancy is the warning sign, not the weakness
Whole-spine MRI is required because multilevel disease is common
Dexamethasone is given before imaging, not after it
Function at the time of treatment predicts function afterwards
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone 16 mg daily is started at the moment cord compression is suspected in cancer, and whole-spine MRI should be obtained within 24 hours because up to one third of patients have compression at a second level.

subtopic_detail: Responding to a family request for artificial hydration in the last days of life
stem:
An 88-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer is in a palliative care unit and is recognised to be in her last days of life. She has taken only sips of water for three days and has been unrousable since yesterday morning.

Her son has driven from interstate and is distressed. He asks you to start a drip, saying he cannot bear the thought of his mother dying thirsty.

Her lips and tongue are dry, she is not grimacing or restless, and there has been no jerking of her limbs. She is on a continuous subcutaneous infusion of morphine that has kept her settled for the past 48 hours, with no breakthrough doses required overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 12/min, SpO2 not measured, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No peripheral oedema and no added breath sounds

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Start subcutaneous fluid at one litre over 24 hours and review the effect daily
options.rationale: Subcutaneous fluid does not relieve the sensation of dry mouth and, in a dying patient with falling albumin, adds to respiratory secretions and peripheral oedema; a short trial is defensible only when dehydration is contributing to a reversible delirium. (Source: NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation: Last Days of Life Toolkit)
source_refs: NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation: Last Days of Life Toolkit

options.text: Start intravenous fluid at 80 mL per hour and monitor her for peripheral oedema
options.rationale: Intravenous access in a dying patient adds an invasive procedure without symptom benefit, and this rate exceeds what a failing circulation will distribute. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Provide regular mouth care and sips as tolerated, with explanation for family
options.rationale: The sensation of thirst in the dying is driven by dry oral mucosa rather than by circulating volume, so frequent mouth care relieves it while artificial hydration does not; explaining this to the family is part of the intervention, not an alternative to it. (Source: NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation: Last Days of Life Toolkit)
source_refs: NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation: Last Days of Life Toolkit

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube for hydration and continue it until she is more alert
options.rationale: Nasogastric hydration is burdensome, carries aspiration risk in an unrousable patient, and the premise that she will become more alert is not realistic at this stage. (Source: Palliative Care Australia)

options.text: Check her urea and electrolytes and decide on fluid once the results are back
options.rationale: Blood tests in the last days of life do not change symptom-directed management and the venepuncture itself is a burden; investigation here substitutes for a conversation. (Source: NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation: Last Days of Life Toolkit)
source_refs: NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation: Last Days of Life Toolkit

explanation.summary: Requests for fluid at the end of life are usually requests for reassurance that the patient is not suffering, and they are best answered by addressing the symptom rather than the biochemistry. Randomised evidence in advanced cancer shows no improvement in thirst, delirium or survival with subcutaneous hydration, while fluid loading worsens respiratory secretions, oedema and vomiting in bowel obstruction. Mouth care every one to two hours, lip balm and ice chips are the effective treatment for dry mouth. A time-limited trial of subcutaneous fluid remains reasonable when dehydration is a plausible contributor to a potentially reversible delirium, with agreed review points. In context, a family's request at the end of life is usually a request for reassurance, and the answer is to treat the symptom and explain the reasoning rather than to order the intervention.
key_points: Thirst at the end of life correlates with dry mucosa, not with hydration status
Artificial hydration does not improve thirst, delirium or survival in advanced cancer
Excess fluid worsens secretions, oedema and obstructive vomiting
Explaining the reasoning to family is an essential part of the management
explanation.pearls: Mouth care every one to two hours with an oral sponge and lip balm relieves end-of-life thirst more reliably than a litre of subcutaneous fluid, and can be taught to family members who want to help.

sources.label: NSW Agency for Clinical Innovation: Last Days of Life Toolkit

subtopic_detail: Rationalising the medication chart when swallowing is lost in the last days of life
stem:
You visit a 90-year-old man in his residential aged care facility. He has metastatic lung cancer and over the past week has become bed-bound and drowsy, rousing only briefly when his daughter speaks to him. The facility staff report that this morning he coughed and spluttered on his crushed tablets and refused any further medicines.

His current chart is perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, alendronate 70 mg weekly, metformin 500 mg twice daily, aspirin 100 mg daily, slow-release morphine 20 mg twice daily and a daily macrogol sachet.

He grimaces when the staff roll him. His daughter and the facility both wish him to remain there rather than return to hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 93% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Rouses briefly to voice, unable to swallow safely, no urine output recorded for 12 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication plan?

options.text: Cease the whole oral regimen and chart subcutaneous morphine with as-required medicines
options.rationale: When swallowing is lost in the last days, medicines with no symptom benefit in that timeframe are stopped and essential symptom control is converted to the subcutaneous route, with as-required medicines charted in advance for pain, breathlessness, nausea, secretions and agitation. (Source: caring@home (palliative care subcutaneous medicines project))

options.text: Continue all his current medicines by crushing them and giving them in thickened fluid
options.rationale: Crushing in thickened fluid risks aspiration in a patient who is already coughing on his medicines, and none of the preventive agents will benefit him in the days remaining. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Palliative and end-of-life care)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Palliative and end-of-life care

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube so that his oral regimen can be continued without change
options.rationale: A nasogastric tube is a burdensome intervention to deliver drugs whose time to benefit is measured in years, and it conflicts with the plan to keep him where he is. (Source: Palliative Care Australia)

options.text: Cease only the statin and the bisphosphonate and continue the other oral medicines
options.rationale: Stopping the two longest time-to-benefit drugs is a step in the right direction but leaves him swallowing tablets he cannot manage and leaves his pain relief on an unusable route. (Source: Primary Health Tasmania: A Guide to Deprescribing)
source_refs: Primary Health Tasmania: A Guide to Deprescribing

options.text: Chart subcutaneous morphine but continue his oral cardiac and diabetes medicines unchanged
options.rationale: This gets the analgesic route right but retains antihypertensive and glucose-lowering agents that now risk symptomatic hypotension and hypoglycaemia in a patient with negligible intake. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

explanation.summary: Recognising dying triggers a specific set of prescribing decisions: stop what cannot help in the time remaining, convert what is still needed to a usable route, and chart anticipatory medicines before the symptom appears so that nobody has to wait for a doctor at 3 am. In Australian residential aged care the subcutaneous route is the standard alternative when swallowing fails, delivered by intermittent injection through an indwelling subcutaneous cannula or by continuous infusion. Statins, bisphosphonates, antihypertensives, oral hypoglycaemics and antiplatelets all have time to benefit far longer than the prognosis and are ceased. Anticipatory prescribing is what most often prevents an avoidable transfer to hospital. In context, recognising that a patient is dying is itself a prescribing decision, and every drug on the chart is then judged against the time that remains.
key_points: Time to benefit is the test for continuing any preventive medicine at the end of life
Loss of swallowing is the trigger to convert essential symptom medicines to subcutaneous
Anticipatory as-required medicines cover pain, breathlessness, nausea, secretions and agitation
Continuing antihypertensives and hypoglycaemics in a dying patient causes symptoms, not benefit
explanation.pearls: An indwelling subcutaneous cannula sited in the upper chest or abdomen can be left in place for up to seven days and lets aged care staff give as-required symptom medicines without repeated needle insertions.

sources.label: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Palliative and end-of-life care
Primary Health Tasmania: A Guide to Deprescribing

subtopic_detail: Predictable procedure-related pain on a stable background opioid
stem:
A 74-year-old woman with locally advanced breast cancer attends the community palliative care clinic. Her chest wall wound is dressed twice weekly by the district nurses.

For the past month her background pain has been controlled on her current slow-release opioid, and she has used no more than one breakthrough dose a week. She reads and gardens between dressing changes and is not drowsy.

During each dressing change she cries out and asks the nurses to stop, and she is tearful for the rest of the visit. Within 20 minutes of the dressing being finished she is comfortable again and back to her usual self.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Slow-release morphine 30 mg twice daily, immediate-release morphine 10 mg as required, macrogol daily, paracetamol 1 g four times daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her analgesia?

options.text: Increase her slow-release morphine to 60 mg twice daily and review weekly
options.rationale: Doubling the background dose to cover two brief episodes a week will sedate her for the 165 hours in between, when her pain is already controlled. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic)

options.text: Add regular paracetamol four times daily and continue her current opioid regimen
options.rationale: She is already taking regular paracetamol, so this changes nothing and leaves the procedural pain untreated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Add slow-release oxycodone 10 mg twice daily alongside her current morphine dose
options.rationale: Running two long-acting opioids together compounds the background dose and makes future titration and conversion unsafe; if a rotation were indicated, one drug would replace the other. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic)

options.text: Give an immediate-release morphine dose half an hour before each dressing
options.rationale: Incident pain that is predictable, brief and superimposed on well-controlled background pain is treated by timing a short-acting opioid to the trigger; oral immediate-release morphine peaks at 30 to 60 minutes, which matches the dressing change. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Add regular amitriptyline 10 mg at night and reassess after the next dressing
options.rationale: Tricyclic adjuvants are for neuropathic pain and take days to weeks to work, which does not match brief procedure-triggered nociceptive pain. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Breakthrough pain divides into three patterns that are managed differently: end-of-dose failure, which needs the background dose or interval adjusted; spontaneous idiopathic pain, which needs as-required analgesia available; and incident pain, which is predictable and is best pre-empted. Pre-emptive dosing timed to the peak effect of the formulation is the key manoeuvre for incident pain, and it avoids the sedation and constipation that come from escalating a background dose that is already adequate. Non-drug measures matter too: soaking adherent dressings, using atraumatic contact layers, and allowing the patient to call a pause. The as-required dose is conventionally one sixth of the total daily oral morphine equivalent. In context, matching the analgesic strategy to the temporal pattern of the pain avoids sedating a patient all week for a problem that lasts 20 minutes twice.
key_points: Distinguish incident, spontaneous and end-of-dose breakthrough pain before changing anything
Well-controlled background pain is a reason not to raise the long-acting dose
Oral immediate-release morphine peaks at 30 to 60 minutes; give it before the trigger
Never run two slow-release opioids concurrently
explanation.pearls: The as-required breakthrough dose is one sixth of the total 24-hour oral morphine equivalent, so a patient on 60 mg of slow-release morphine daily is prescribed 10 mg of immediate-release morphine per dose.

subtopic_detail: Non-pharmacological management of chronic breathlessness without hypoxaemia
stem:
A 76-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and metastatic lung cancer is seen at home by the community palliative care service. He has been breathless at rest for three weeks and can no longer walk to his letterbox.

He was started on immediate-release morphine 2.5 mg four-hourly a fortnight ago and reports that it takes the edge off but that he still panics when the breathlessness comes on. His daughter has bought a second-hand oxygen concentrator and wants to know when to turn it on.

His chest is quiet with a prolonged expiratory phase and there is no new focal change. He is not using accessory muscles at rest and speaks in full sentences.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mild ankle oedema, no calf tenderness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Arrange home oxygen at 2 litres per minute by nasal prongs for continuous use
options.rationale: Oxygen relieves breathlessness only in patients who are hypoxaemic, and at an SpO2 of 95 per cent it performs no better than air from a fan while adding cost, tethering and fire risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Provide a handheld fan directed at the face with breathing and positioning advice
options.rationale: Cool airflow across the second and third trigeminal nerve distributions reduces the sensation of breathlessness within minutes and is the first-line non-drug measure, combined with pursed-lip breathing, forward-lean positioning and an action plan for panic. (Source: Palliative Care Australia)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 25 mg daily for five days and review his symptoms after
options.rationale: A corticosteroid course treats an exacerbation, and there is no wheeze, sputum change or new focal finding to support one here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Start regular diazepam 2 mg three times daily for his breathlessness-related anxiety
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are third-line for refractory breathlessness after opioids and non-drug measures have been optimised, and regular long-acting dosing in an older man risks sedation and falls. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Increase his morphine to 10 mg four-hourly and review the effect in 48 hours
options.rationale: A fourfold jump overshoots the usual titration, which proceeds in increments of 25 to 50 per cent, and it leaves the panic component untreated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Chronic refractory breathlessness is managed with a combination of non-pharmacological measures and low-dose opioids, in that order of first reach. Randomised evidence shows a handheld fan is as effective as oxygen in non-hypoxaemic patients and works within minutes at no cost. Low-dose oral morphine reduces the intensity of breathlessness without respiratory depression at palliative doses, titrated slowly. Anxiety and breathlessness amplify each other, so breathing retraining, positioning and a written plan for episodes address a component that neither oxygen nor opioids reach. In context, non-drug measures in refractory breathlessness are not an afterthought to prescribing; they are first-line treatment.
key_points: Oxygen benefits breathlessness only when the patient is hypoxaemic
A handheld fan to the face works within minutes via trigeminal afferents
Low-dose opioids are titrated in 25 to 50 per cent increments, not by fourfold jumps
Benzodiazepines sit third-line, after non-drug measures and opioids
explanation.pearls: A handheld fan held about 15 cm from the face and aimed at the central cheeks and nose reduces breathlessness within minutes and matches oxygen in patients whose SpO2 is above 92 per cent.

subtopic_detail: Compounded bleeding risk from a recently added agent
stem:
A 77-year-old woman attends for a routine review. She has atrial fibrillation treated with apixaban 5 mg twice daily and takes sertraline 50 mg daily for depression, which has been stable for four years.

She mentions that a locum started her on naproxen 500 mg twice daily three weeks ago for pain in her right knee, and that it has helped her walk to the shops again. Since then she has noticed several large bruises on her forearms and some burning discomfort behind her breastbone after meals.

Her stools are described as normal in colour. Her blood pressure today is 148/84 mmHg, up from 128/76 mmHg at her last visit.

data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 118 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 42 mL/min/1.73m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication change?

options.text: Stop apixaban and start aspirin 100 mg daily with a proton pump inhibitor
options.rationale: Aspirin gives little stroke protection in atrial fibrillation while retaining bleeding risk, and removing the anticoagulant to keep the analgesic inverts the risk-benefit balance. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Australian clinical guidelines for the diagnosis and management of atrial fibrillation)
source_refs: NHFA/CSANZ Australian clinical guidelines for the diagnosis and management of atrial fibrillation

options.text: Continue all her medicines and add pantoprazole 20 mg daily with a repeat count
options.rationale: Gastric protection reduces upper gastrointestinal injury but does nothing about the renal impairment, the blood pressure rise or the platelet effect, so the underlying hazard persists. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Switch sertraline to mirtazapine and continue naproxen at a reduced daily dose
options.rationale: Changing an antidepressant that has been effective for four years targets the smallest contributor while leaving the recently added and most modifiable one in place. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Switch naproxen to celecoxib 100 mg daily and add pantoprazole 20 mg daily
options.rationale: A selective cyclo-oxygenase-2 inhibitor lowers gastric but not renal or cardiovascular risk, and any oral anti-inflammatory remains inappropriate at an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 42 on an anticoagulant. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Stop naproxen and manage the knee pain with paracetamol and topical therapy
options.rationale: The anti-inflammatory is the newest addition and the one driving bruising, dyspepsia, the blood pressure rise and the fall in renal function on top of an anticoagulant and a serotonergic agent; topical anti-inflammatory and paracetamol give knee-specific benefit with minimal systemic absorption. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Polypharmacy)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Polypharmacy

explanation.summary: The combination of an anticoagulant, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug and a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is a recognised high-risk triple, because each acts on a different limb of haemostasis: coagulation, platelet cyclo-oxygenase and platelet serotonin uptake. Oral anti-inflammatory drugs in older people also raise blood pressure, precipitate acute kidney injury and worsen heart failure, and they appear on Australian deprescribing and Choosing Wisely lists for this reason. When a new symptom follows a new drug, the new drug is the first thing to examine. Topical anti-inflammatory preparations achieve useful local concentrations for knee osteoarthritis with roughly 5 per cent of the systemic exposure. In context, a new symptom in an older patient is a medication question until the medication list has been examined.
key_points: Anticoagulant plus anti-inflammatory plus serotonergic antidepressant multiplies bleeding risk
Oral anti-inflammatory drugs raise blood pressure and reduce glomerular filtration in older people
The most recently started medicine is the first suspect for a new symptom
Topical anti-inflammatory therapy is an evidence-supported substitute for knee osteoarthritis
explanation.pearls: Topical diclofenac applied to the knee produces about 5 per cent of the systemic exposure of an equivalent oral dose, which is why it is preferred when an older patient is anticoagulated or has an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 60.

sources.label: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Polypharmacy
NHFA/CSANZ Australian clinical guidelines for the diagnosis and management of atrial fibrillation

subtopic_detail: Choosing the first medicine to stop using time to benefit
stem:
An 84-year-old man with metastatic colorectal cancer is reviewed in the outpatient clinic. Systemic treatment was stopped last month and the oncology team estimate his prognosis in months rather than years.

He spends more than half his waking hours in a chair or in bed and needs help to shower. He tells you he is tired of swallowing so many tablets each day and asks which ones he can let go.

He has aching thighs on most days and no history of vascular disease. His bone pain is well controlled and his bowels open daily. He has never had a fracture or a myocardial infarction.

data_table.Medications: Atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, pantoprazole 20 mg daily, paracetamol 1 g four times daily, colecalciferol 1000 IU daily, macrogol one sachet daily, slow-release oxycodone 10 mg twice daily
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110), liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: Which medicine is most appropriate to cease first?

options.text: Pantoprazole 20 mg daily, which was started for reflux during his recent chemotherapy
options.rationale: Long-term proton pump inhibitors are a legitimate deprescribing target, but this one still has a plausible symptomatic indication and stopping it risks rebound acid symptoms; it is a later step. (Source: Primary Health Tasmania: A Guide to Deprescribing)
source_refs: Primary Health Tasmania: A Guide to Deprescribing

options.text: Paracetamol 1 g four times daily, taken for his background bone pain
options.rationale: Paracetamol provides same-day symptom benefit and is opioid-sparing; stopping it would increase his opioid requirement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, which was prescribed years ago for primary prevention
options.rationale: The time to any cardiovascular benefit from a primary-prevention statin is two to five years, well beyond his prognosis, and a randomised trial in advanced illness showed stopping improved quality of life without raising mortality; his thigh aching may also be drug-related. (Source: Primary Health Tasmania: A Guide to Deprescribing)
source_refs: Primary Health Tasmania: A Guide to Deprescribing

options.text: Colecalciferol 1000 IU daily, which was prescribed for his bone health
options.rationale: Vitamin D is a reasonable later candidate but it is one small capsule with a possible role in muscle function; the higher-burden, longer time-to-benefit agent goes first. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Polypharmacy)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Polypharmacy

options.text: Macrogol one sachet daily, which was prescribed alongside his regular opioid
options.rationale: Aperients prescribed with a regular opioid are preventing a symptom that will return within days of stopping, so this is the wrong direction entirely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

explanation.summary: Deprescribing in limited prognosis is driven by time to benefit: a drug whose benefit accrues over years cannot help a patient whose prognosis is months, while its adverse effects and swallowing burden are immediate. Statins for primary prevention are the archetype, with a randomised discontinuation trial in advanced life-limiting illness showing better quality of life and no excess mortality. The counterpart principle is that symptom-control and symptom-prevention medicines are protected, including aperients prescribed with opioids. Deprescribing conversations work best when the patient sets the agenda, as here, and when the plan names one drug at a time with a review point. In context, deprescribing is not a withdrawal of care but the substitution of drugs that can still help for drugs that no longer can.
key_points: Time to benefit versus remaining prognosis is the primary deprescribing test
Primary-prevention statins take two to five years to yield benefit
Symptom-control and symptom-prevention medicines are protected from deprescribing
Stop one medicine at a time and set a review date
explanation.pearls: Stopping a statin in advanced life-limiting illness improved quality of life with no increase in 60-day mortality in a randomised trial, which is why it is the standard first medicine to cease when prognosis is months.

sources.label: Primary Health Tasmania: A Guide to Deprescribing
RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Polypharmacy

subtopic_detail: Reviewing long-term antiresorptive therapy after five years
stem:
A 76-year-old woman asks whether she still needs the weekly tablet she has taken since a wrist fracture at the age of 70. She has taken alendronate 70 mg weekly for five and a half years and has not missed a dose.

She walks 3 km most days, has never taken a corticosteroid, and has had no fracture since the wrist. Her height is unchanged on measurement today.

She had repeat densitometry last month and asks whether the result changes anything.

data_table.Investigations: Femoral neck T-score -1.9 (pre-treatment -2.6), lumbar spine T-score -1.7, corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 76 nmol/L (>50)
data_table.Medications: Alendronate 70 mg weekly, colecalciferol 1000 IU daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her osteoporosis therapy?

options.text: Stop alendronate now and reassess her fracture risk with densitometry in two years
options.rationale: After five years of oral bisphosphonate, a patient with no fracture on treatment and a femoral neck T-score above -2.5 is at low risk and can take a drug holiday, with reassessment because the skeletal effect wanes over two to three years. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management position statement)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management position statement

options.text: Continue alendronate indefinitely on the basis that her fracture risk remains elevated
options.rationale: Continuing beyond five years is reserved for patients who remain high risk, and open-ended therapy adds atypical femoral fracture and osteonecrosis risk without demonstrated benefit in this group. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management position statement)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management position statement

options.text: Switch to denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every six months and continue indefinitely
options.rationale: Denosumab is a step up in potency for patients with continuing high risk, and it cannot simply be stopped later because discontinuation causes rebound bone loss and vertebral fractures. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Switch to daily teriparatide for 18 months and then review her bone mineral density
options.rationale: Anabolic therapy is for severe osteoporosis with fractures on antiresorptive treatment, which is the opposite of her trajectory. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Stop alendronate now and start calcium 1200 mg daily with no further bone review
options.rationale: Stopping is right but discharging her from review is not, and high-dose calcium supplements add cardiovascular and renal stone concerns without fracture benefit when dietary intake is adequate. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management position statement)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management position statement

explanation.summary: Bisphosphonates bind to bone and continue to act after dosing stops, which creates the option of a drug holiday that does not exist for denosumab. Australian practice is to review oral bisphosphonate therapy at five years and intravenous therapy at three, then to stratify: patients with a fracture on treatment, a hip or spine T-score at or below -2.5, or ongoing corticosteroid exposure continue, while lower-risk patients stop and are reassessed in one to three years. Denosumab is the important exception, where cessation without a bisphosphonate to follow causes a rapid rebound in bone turnover and multiple vertebral fractures within a year. Calcium is preferably obtained from diet, with supplements reserved for demonstrated inadequacy. In context, long-term preventive therapy earns a scheduled review rather than indefinite repeat prescribing.
key_points: Review oral bisphosphonate therapy at five years and intravenous therapy at three
No fracture on treatment plus T-score above -2.5 supports a drug holiday
Bisphosphonate effect persists for two to three years after cessation
Denosumab must never be stopped without follow-on antiresorptive cover
explanation.pearls: Stopping denosumab without a follow-on bisphosphonate causes rebound vertebral fractures within 9 to 18 months, so the next dose is due no later than seven months after the previous one.

sources.label: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management position statement
RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Polypharmacy

subtopic_detail: Stopping a cholinesterase inhibitor when the treatment goal can no longer be met
stem:
You review an 89-year-old woman in her residential aged care facility at the request of her family. She has had Alzheimer dementia for nine years and has taken donepezil daily for the last six.

She no longer uses words, does not recognise her daughter, and is fully dependent for feeding, transfers and continence. Her daughter asks whether the tablets are still doing anything.

Staff report she has lost 6 kg over six months and often refuses food. Her pulse has been persistently low at each of the last three facility observations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 48/min regular, blood pressure 118/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Medications: Donepezil 10 mg daily, paracetamol 1 g three times daily, colecalciferol 1000 IU daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her donepezil?

options.text: Increase donepezil to 15 mg daily and monitor her cognition over three months
options.rationale: There is no 15 mg strength in Australia and no cognitive gain to pursue at this stage; raising the dose would deepen the bradycardia and anorexia. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Switch to rivastigmine patch 9.5 mg daily to reduce gastrointestinal adverse effects
options.rationale: Rivastigmine is the same pharmacological class, so the cholinergic bradycardia and anorexia persist; a transdermal switch addresses nausea, which is not the problem here. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Add memantine 10 mg twice daily and continue donepezil at her current dose
options.rationale: Adding a second agent increases burden and cost when the treatment goal is no longer achievable, and combination therapy has not been shown to change outcomes at this severity. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Dementia)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Dementia

options.text: Taper and cease donepezil, monitoring her for any deterioration over four weeks
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors are stopped when the goal of therapy can no longer be met, and her bradycardia and weight loss are recognised cholinergic adverse effects; tapering over two to four weeks with review allows the drug to be restarted if function clearly declines. (Source: Primary Health Tasmania: A Guide to Deprescribing)
source_refs: Primary Health Tasmania: A Guide to Deprescribing

options.text: Continue donepezil unchanged and refer her for 24-hour ambulatory cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Investigating drug-induced bradycardia while continuing the causative drug inverts the order; the diagnostic and therapeutic test is withdrawal. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Cholinesterase inhibitors give a modest symptomatic benefit in mild to moderate Alzheimer dementia and do not modify the disease. Continuation is reviewed against the original goal, and when a patient is non-verbal and fully dependent that goal is no longer attainable. Cholinergic adverse effects accumulate quietly over years: bradycardia, syncope, weight loss, anorexia, nausea, urinary urgency and vivid dreams, and the bradycardia is associated with falls, pacemaker insertion and hip fracture. Tapering rather than abrupt cessation, with a defined review window, distinguishes genuine withdrawal decline from the underlying disease trajectory. In context, every long-term medicine needs a stated goal, because a goal that can no longer be reached is the clearest indication to stop.
key_points: Cholinesterase inhibitors are symptomatic, not disease-modifying
Bradycardia, weight loss and anorexia are class adverse effects that emerge slowly
Stop when the treatment goal can no longer be met, not at a fixed dementia stage
Taper over two to four weeks and review, so a real decline can be distinguished
explanation.pearls: Donepezil-associated bradycardia below 50 beats per minute is a recognised cause of syncope and hip fracture in aged care residents, and typically resolves within two to four weeks of cessation.

sources.label: Primary Health Tasmania: A Guide to Deprescribing
RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Dementia

subtopic_detail: Reversible metabolic cause of deterioration in advanced malignancy
stem:
A 71-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer involving the spine and pelvis is brought in by her husband. Over five days she has become progressively drowsy, has vomited several times a day and has not opened her bowels for a week.

He says she has been drinking glass after glass of water and getting up at night to pass urine, which is new.

She is rousable and orientated to person only. Her mucous membranes are dry and her skin turgor is reduced. Her opioid dose has not changed for six weeks and her pupils are 3 mm and reactive.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 102/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 3.28 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), albumin 30 g/L (34-48), creatinine 132 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 36 mL/min/1.73m2, sodium 141 mmol/L (135-145)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Give intravenous frusemide 40 mg after a 500 mL saline bolus and recheck
options.rationale: Loop diuretics were once used to force calciuresis but worsen the volume depletion that is driving the hypercalcaemia; they are reserved for fluid overload during rehydration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Give intravenous sodium chloride 0.9% rehydration first and then zoledronic acid
options.rationale: Restoring intravascular volume first improves glomerular filtration and calcium excretion and protects the kidney from the bisphosphonate, which is then given to inhibit the osteoclastic bone resorption driving the calcium; zoledronic acid takes two to four days to reach maximal effect. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Start oral prednisolone 50 mg daily and restrict her dietary calcium intake
options.rationale: Corticosteroids lower calcium in vitamin D-mediated states such as lymphoma and sarcoidosis, not in osteolytic or parathyroid hormone-related peptide mediated malignancy, and dietary restriction has no meaningful effect. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Start subcutaneous calcitonin alone and repeat her serum calcium in 48 hours
options.rationale: Calcitonin works within hours but tachyphylaxis develops in 48 hours, so it is an adjunct for severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia rather than a stand-alone treatment. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Start denosumab 120 mg subcutaneously without first giving any intravenous rehydration
options.rationale: Denosumab is an option in bisphosphonate-refractory hypercalcaemia or severe renal impairment, but giving any antiresorptive without first correcting volume depletion leaves the renal impairment untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

explanation.summary: Hypercalcaemia occurs in up to a fifth of patients with advanced cancer, most often breast, myeloma, lung and renal primaries, and its symptoms overlap closely with opioid toxicity and with dying: drowsiness, confusion, nausea, constipation and polyuria. Missing it means missing one of the few readily reversible causes of deterioration in palliative care, and treating it can restore weeks of function. Volume repletion with normal saline comes first because the polyuria causes dehydration that itself impairs calcium excretion, then an intravenous bisphosphonate reduces bone resorption over several days. Recurrence is common and each episode is a marker of poor prognosis, which makes it a natural point to revisit goals of care. In context, deterioration in advanced cancer deserves a short search for a reversible cause before it is accepted as the disease trajectory.
key_points: Polyuria, drowsiness, nausea and constipation together suggest hypercalcaemia in malignancy
Rehydration precedes any antiresorptive therapy and protects renal function
Zoledronic acid takes two to four days for maximal calcium lowering
The symptom picture mimics opioid toxicity and the dying process
explanation.pearls: Zoledronic acid reaches its maximal calcium-lowering effect at two to four days, so calcitonin is added when severe symptoms demand a fall within hours.

subtopic_detail: Localised metastatic bone pain not responding to opioid escalation
stem:
A 70-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer reports worsening pain over his right hip for six weeks. It is worst when he puts weight through the leg and eases when he sits.

His slow-release morphine has been tripled over that period. He now sleeps through visits from his grandchildren and his daughter says he is not himself, yet he still rates the hip pain at 8 out of 10 on standing.

Pain is reproduced by percussion over the right greater trochanter and there is no pain elsewhere. A recent bone scan showed increased uptake at that site with no other new lesion.

data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.36 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 84 micromol/L (60-110), haemoglobin 116 g/L (130-180)
data_table.Medications: Slow-release morphine 90 mg twice daily, immediate-release morphine 30 mg as required, macrogol daily, paracetamol 1 g four times daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in managing his pain?

options.text: Increase his slow-release morphine by a further 50 per cent and add more aperients
options.rationale: Three dose increases have produced sedation without analgesia, which is the signature of a pain that is not opioid-responsive; a fourth will deepen the toxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Add regular pregabalin 75 mg twice daily and review his response in two weeks
options.rationale: Gabapentinoids target neuropathic pain, and there is no radicular radiation, dysaesthesia or sensory change here to support that mechanism. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Start dexamethasone 8 mg daily and continue his current opioid doses unchanged
options.rationale: A corticosteroid can give short-term relief in bone pain but is an adjunct rather than the definitive treatment, and long-term use brings myopathy, delirium and hyperglycaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Rotate from morphine to hydromorphone at an equianalgesic dose reduced by a third
options.rationale: Rotation helps when toxicity dominates on a dose that is otherwise effective, but it will not make a localised metastatic deposit responsive to systemic opioid alone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic)

options.text: Refer him for palliative external beam radiotherapy directed at the painful site
options.rationale: Localised, weight-bearing, percussion-tender metastatic bone pain that has escalated past useful opioid doses is the standard indication for palliative radiotherapy, which gives partial relief in about 60 per cent of patients; a single fraction is as effective as multifraction courses for uncomplicated bone metastases. (Source: eviQ Radiation Oncology: Bone metastases (palliative))

explanation.summary: Metastatic bone pain is only partly opioid-responsive, and the clue that a different modality is needed is escalating opioid producing sedation without analgesia. Palliative external beam radiotherapy relieves pain in around 60 per cent of treated sites, with onset usually within two to four weeks, and a single 8 Gy fraction matches longer courses for uncomplicated metastases while being far easier for a frail patient to attend. Pain that is worse on weight bearing also raises the question of impending pathological fracture, which is an orthopaedic referral rather than a radiotherapy one. Bone-modifying agents such as zoledronic acid or denosumab reduce skeletal events over months but are not an analgesic answer for this week. In context, pain that stops responding to dose escalation is indicating a change of modality rather than a change of number.
key_points: Sedation without analgesia on rising opioid doses signals incomplete opioid responsiveness
Palliative radiotherapy relieves about 60 per cent of painful bone metastases
Weight-bearing pain raises the question of impending pathological fracture
Bone-modifying agents prevent skeletal events; they do not provide rapid analgesia
explanation.pearls: A single 8 Gy fraction gives equivalent pain relief to multifraction radiotherapy for uncomplicated bone metastases, with retreatment possible if pain recurs.

subtopic_detail: Vitamin D repletion and exercise prescription in a recurrent faller
stem:
An 82-year-old woman has had two falls in the past six months, both indoors and neither causing a fracture. She lives alone, rarely goes outside during winter and covers her arms and legs when she does.

She takes perindopril 5 mg daily and no sedatives. Lying and standing blood pressures show no postural drop and her visual acuity is 6/9 with her current glasses.

She can rise from a chair only by pushing on the armrests, and her timed up-and-go is 16 seconds. She tells you her neighbour was given a large once-a-year vitamin D dose and asks whether she should have the same.

data_table.Investigations: 25-hydroxyvitamin D 38 nmol/L (>50 sufficient), corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 62 mL/min/1.73m2, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Colecalciferol 1000 IU daily plus referral to a supervised balance and strength class
options.rationale: Her level is below the Australian sufficiency threshold of 50 nmol/L so daily repletion is indicated, but the intervention that actually reduces falls is supervised progressive balance and strength training; the two are prescribed together. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Vitamin D and health in adults position statement)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia: Vitamin D and health in adults position statement

options.text: Colecalciferol 500,000 IU orally as a single annual dose, with clinical review in 12 months
options.rationale: A single high annual dose increased falls and fractures in a randomised trial of older women, particularly in the three months after dosing, and is not recommended. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Vitamin D and health in adults position statement)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia: Vitamin D and health in adults position statement

options.text: Colecalciferol 1000 IU daily alone, with repeat vitamin D testing in three months
options.rationale: Correcting the deficiency without prescribing exercise omits the only intervention with consistent falls reduction, and routine repeat testing after uncomplicated repletion is low value. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls

options.text: Referral to a supervised balance and strength class with no vitamin D treatment
options.rationale: The exercise half is right, but leaving a measured level of 38 nmol/L untreated in a housebound woman ignores a documented deficiency with musculoskeletal consequences. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Vitamin D and health in adults position statement)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia: Vitamin D and health in adults position statement

options.text: Calcium carbonate 1200 mg daily with colecalciferol 1000 IU daily and hazard review
options.rationale: Routine calcium supplementation adds gastrointestinal and possible cardiovascular harm without falls benefit when dietary intake is adequate, and home hazard review helps only high-risk fallers as part of a wider programme. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management position statement)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management position statement

explanation.summary: Falls prevention in community-dwelling older people rests on supervised progressive balance and strength training, with the strongest effect seen in programmes delivering at least 50 hours in total and challenging balance rather than walking alone. Vitamin D has a much narrower role: correct measured deficiency below 50 nmol/L, but do not expect supplementation alone to prevent falls in replete people, and avoid intermittent high-dose regimens, which have increased falls and fractures in randomised trials. In Australia, sufficiency is defined as a 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of at least 50 nmol/L at the end of winter, with 1000 to 2000 IU daily the usual maintenance dose. Multifactorial assessment adds medication review, postural blood pressure, vision and footwear. In context, correcting a deficiency and reducing falls are two different tasks, and only one of them is achieved with a supplement.
key_points: Supervised balance and strength training is the highest-yield falls intervention
Australian vitamin D sufficiency is a level of at least 50 nmol/L
Annual or intermittent high-dose vitamin D increases falls and fractures
Calcium supplementation does not prevent falls when dietary intake is adequate
explanation.pearls: A single annual 500,000 IU dose of colecalciferol increased falls by about 15 per cent in a randomised trial of older Australian women, with the excess concentrated in the three months after dosing.

sources.label: Healthy Bones Australia: Vitamin D and health in adults position statement
Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management position statement
RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls

subtopic_detail: Separating a cardiac cause from a mechanical fall
stem:
A 79-year-old man is brought to your clinic by his wife after his third fall in four months. On this occasion she found him on the kitchen floor and he has no memory of going down.

She says he looked grey and clammy for about a minute and then talked to her normally. He was talking normally within a minute and had no limb jerking. Two of the earlier falls happened while he was carrying washing to the line.

His pulse has a slow upstroke and there is an ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge that radiates to both carotids.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min regular, blood pressure 126/82 mmHg supine and 124/80 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 138 g/L (130-180), creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer him to a community falls prevention programme and review in three months
options.rationale: Exercise programmes are the right answer for mechanical falls, but an unwitnessed collapse with pallor and rapid full recovery needs a cardiac cause excluded before he is sent to a gym. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls

options.text: Arrange outpatient 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring and review the resulting trace
options.rationale: Ambulatory blood pressure detects postural and postprandial hypotension, and his bedside lying and standing readings are already flat, so this is chasing a mechanism the examination has argued against. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls

options.text: Arrange an urgent transthoracic echocardiogram today with a resting 12-lead electrocardiogram
options.rationale: Exertional collapse with pallor, rapid recovery and a slow-rising pulse with a murmur radiating to the carotids indicates an outflow obstruction requiring urgent structural assessment, and the electrocardiogram simultaneously screens for conduction disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Arrange a non-contrast CT brain with carotid duplex ultrasound within one week
options.rationale: Transient global loss of consciousness is very rarely cerebrovascular, and carotid disease causes focal deficit rather than collapse with immediate full recovery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Arrange a tilt-table test and refer him to the syncope clinic next month
options.rationale: Tilt testing evaluates suspected reflex syncope and is contraindicated as a first step when structural or arrhythmic causes are unexcluded; a six-week delay is unsafe with exertional symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Around a third of falls in older people are unwitnessed, and a proportion of those labelled mechanical are actually syncopal, because retrograde amnesia for the event is common. The features that redirect the workup are exertional timing, pallor, absence of post-event confusion, and rapid complete recovery, and the examination findings that matter are the pulse character, murmurs and the lying and standing blood pressure. Structural outflow obstruction and bradyarrhythmia are the two high-risk causes to exclude before any rehabilitation referral, because both carry a risk of sudden death and both are treatable. Falls assessment and syncope assessment overlap heavily in this age group and should be done together rather than sequentially. In context, falls assessment and syncope assessment in older people are a single task, because the patient often cannot say which one happened.
key_points: Amnesia for the fall means syncope has not been excluded
Exertional collapse with pallor and fast recovery points to a cardiac mechanism
A slow-rising pulse with a murmur radiating to the carotids demands urgent echocardiography
Tilt testing is for suspected reflex syncope after structural causes are excluded
explanation.pearls: Exertional syncope with a slow-rising pulse carries an average survival of around two to three years without intervention, which makes it one of the few falls presentations requiring assessment within days.
