ANZSGM position statement on comprehensive geriatric assessment

subtopic_detail: Identifying the substitute decision-maker under New South Wales law
stem:
An 85-year-old man with severe dementia is admitted to your New South Wales hospital with aspiration pneumonia. He is drowsy, cannot state where he is and cannot retain or weigh any information about treatment. You need consent for a decision about ongoing intravenous antibiotics and the goals of his care.

A search of his records and his home documents finds no advance care directive and no enduring guardian appointment.

Three relatives are at the bedside. His wife separated from him ten years ago and has not seen him since, though they never divorced. His daughter has lived with him and provided his unpaid daily care for the past three years. His brother visits monthly and holds an enduring power of attorney for financial matters.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104/min, blood pressure 118/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 90% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, coarse crackles at the right base

lead_in: Who should you approach as the substitute decision-maker?

options.text: His brother, because he already holds an enduring power of attorney for this patient
options.rationale: An enduring power of attorney covers financial and legal matters only and confers no authority to consent to medical treatment; a relative who is not the carer also sits below one who is in the hierarchy. (Source: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 (person responsible provisions))

options.text: The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal, by an urgent application for a guardian
options.rationale: Tribunal appointment is needed only when no person responsible can be identified or there is unresolvable conflict, and the delay would be inappropriate when a lawful decision-maker is present at the bedside. (Source: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 (person responsible provisions))

options.text: His wife, because she is his spouse regardless of the current state of the relationship
options.rationale: A spouse ranks highly but only where the relationship is close and continuing, and ten years of separation with no contact does not meet that statutory description. (Source: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 (person responsible provisions))

options.text: His daughter, as the unpaid carer with a close and continuing relationship with him
options.rationale: The New South Wales hierarchy runs guardian, then spouse in a close continuing relationship, then unpaid carer, then close friend or relative; with no guardian and a spouse who no longer qualifies, the daughter who provides his unpaid care is the person responsible. (Source: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 (person responsible provisions))

options.text: The treating team, acting in his best interests without a substitute decision-maker
options.rationale: Clinicians may give urgent treatment necessary to save life or prevent significant distress without consent, but ongoing treatment decisions require the person responsible when one exists. (Source: NSW Health Advance Care Planning policy)
source_refs: NSW Health Advance Care Planning policy

explanation.summary: When an adult lacks capacity in New South Wales, consent for medical treatment comes from the person responsible, identified through a statutory hierarchy rather than by who is loudest or most available. The order is: a guardian with a health function, then a spouse or de facto partner where the relationship is close and continuing, then an unpaid carer, then a close friend or relative. An enduring power of attorney is a financial instrument and an enduring guardian is the health equivalent, a distinction that is frequently confused at the bedside. Urgent treatment to save life or prevent significant pain or distress may proceed without consent, and a valid advance care directive made by the person when they had capacity overrides the person responsible. In context, knowing the local substitute decision-making hierarchy is as much a clinical skill as knowing a drug dose, and it differs between Australian jurisdictions.
key_points: The person responsible hierarchy is guardian, spouse in a close continuing relationship, unpaid carer, then close friend or relative
An enduring power of attorney covers finances, not medical treatment
A separated spouse with no contact does not satisfy the close and continuing test
A valid advance care directive takes precedence over any substitute decision-maker
explanation.pearls: The unpaid carer sits above other relatives in the New South Wales person responsible hierarchy, and receiving a carer payment does not make a carer paid for this purpose.

subtopic_detail: Choosing a starting opioid when glomerular filtration is severely reduced
stem:
An 80-year-old woman with metastatic ovarian cancer describes constant deep abdominal pain rated 7 out of 10 that now wakes her every night. Regular paracetamol 1 g four times daily is no longer helping and she has never taken an opioid.

She lives at home with her daughter, who will supervise her medicines. She weighs 52 kg and eats small amounts.

Her creatinine has risen steadily over three months, attributed to ureteric compression that is not amenable to stenting. She is fully orientated and her liver function is unchanged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 190 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 22 mL/min/1.73m2, potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate analgesic plan?

options.text: Slow-release morphine 10 mg twice daily with immediate-release morphine as required
options.rationale: Morphine-6-glucuronide accumulates when glomerular filtration falls below about 30 mL/min and causes sedation, myoclonus and respiratory depression, and a slow-release formulation removes the ability to stop quickly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Immediate-release oxycodone 2.5 mg four-hourly as required with daily telephone review
options.rationale: Oxycodone has less active renally cleared metabolite accumulation than morphine and is a reasonable choice at reduced dose in severe renal impairment; starting with a low as-required immediate-release dose in an opioid-naive frail woman allows titration against effect before any long-acting preparation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Transdermal fentanyl 12 micrograms per hour with immediate-release morphine as required
options.rationale: Fentanyl is metabolically safe in renal impairment but a patch is contraindicated in opioid-naive patients because it takes 12 to 24 hours to reach effect and cannot be withdrawn quickly; pairing it with morphine also reintroduces the metabolite problem. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Regular ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with paracetamol and weekly review
options.rationale: A non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug at this level of renal function risks precipitating dialysis-requiring failure, and it will not control pain of this severity. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Immediate-release morphine 5 mg four-hourly regularly with aperients and daily review
options.rationale: The formulation and review schedule are appropriate but the drug is not, because regular four-hourly morphine guarantees metabolite accumulation at an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 22. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

explanation.summary: Opioid choice changes when renal function falls, because morphine and codeine depend on renal clearance of active metabolites while fentanyl, buprenorphine, methadone and to a lesser extent oxycodone and hydromorphone do not. Below an estimated glomerular filtration rate of about 30 mL/min, morphine accumulates and produces the picture of drowsiness, myoclonus, pinpoint pupils and hallucinations that is easily mistaken for disease progression. Titration in an opioid-naive frail patient always begins with an immediate-release preparation, as-required or regularly, so that the dose can be adjusted or stopped within hours. Aperients are started with the opioid, not after constipation appears. In context, renal function determines the drug and opioid naivety determines the formulation, and both are settled before a dose is chosen.
key_points: Morphine-6-glucuronide accumulates below an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 30 mL/min
Transdermal patches are contraindicated in opioid-naive patients
Start with an immediate-release preparation so the dose can be adjusted within hours
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are avoided in severe renal impairment
explanation.pearls: Fentanyl and buprenorphine have no clinically significant renally cleared active metabolites, which makes them the preferred long-acting opioids once an opioid-tolerant patient needs a background dose at an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 30.

subtopic_detail: Review of antipsychotic therapy prescribed for behavioural symptoms of dementia
stem:
You are the visiting general practitioner for an 84-year-old woman in residential aged care who has Alzheimer dementia. Sixteen weeks ago she was started on risperidone 0.5 mg twice daily after she hit staff repeatedly during showering.

The care plan shows that showering was moved to the afternoon and a familiar carer assigned at the same time the medicine began. Staff record no episode of aggression for the past ten weeks.

Over the last fortnight she has begun shuffling, her handwriting has become small and she had an unwitnessed fall in the corridor last week. Her weight and swallowing are unchanged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 132/74 mmHg supine and 118/68 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her risperidone?

options.text: Continue risperidone at the current dose and place a movement alarm in her room
options.rationale: Continuing a drug that is producing parkinsonism and managing the resulting falls with monitoring treats the consequence rather than the cause, and the approved treatment period has already been exceeded. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Dementia)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Dementia

options.text: Switch to olanzapine 2.5 mg at night to reduce her extrapyramidal adverse effects
options.rationale: Olanzapine causes less parkinsonism but carries the same class risk of stroke and death in dementia and is not approved for this indication in Australia; substituting one antipsychotic for another avoids the actual decision. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Halve the risperidone dose and schedule the next formal review in twelve months
options.rationale: Dose reduction is a reasonable step but a twelve-month review interval is far outside the recommended timeframe for antipsychotics in dementia, which are reviewed at least every twelve weeks. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Dementia)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Dementia

options.text: Continue risperidone and add benztropine 1 mg daily to treat her gait change
options.rationale: Adding an anticholinergic to counter drug-induced parkinsonism is a prescribing cascade that worsens cognition, causes delirium and increases falls in dementia. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Taper risperidone with a plan to cease it, monitoring her behaviour each week
options.rationale: Risperidone is the only antipsychotic approved in Australia for behavioural symptoms of dementia and only for up to twelve weeks; with ten weeks free of aggression, an effective non-drug strategy in place and emerging parkinsonism, gradual withdrawal with structured behavioural monitoring is indicated. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Dementia)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Dementia

explanation.summary: Antipsychotics in dementia give a small benefit for aggression and psychosis and carry a substantial cost: roughly a 1.5 to 1.7 fold increase in mortality, an increased stroke rate, parkinsonism, sedation and falls. Australian practice restricts risperidone to behavioural and psychological symptoms that persist despite non-drug measures, for a maximum of twelve weeks, with review at least every twelve weeks thereafter if continued. Most residents can be withdrawn without behavioural relapse, particularly when the non-pharmacological measures that were introduced at the same time are maintained. Withdrawal is gradual with weekly behavioural monitoring, and a documented plan for what to do if symptoms return. In context, a drug started for a behaviour needs a planned stop date, because the behaviour that prompted it often resolves while the prescription does not.
key_points: Risperidone is approved in Australia for behavioural symptoms of dementia for up to twelve weeks
Antipsychotics in dementia increase mortality and stroke risk
Drug-induced parkinsonism should prompt withdrawal, not an anticholinergic
Most residents can be withdrawn successfully if non-drug measures are maintained
explanation.pearls: Risperidone carries the only Australian approval for behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia, limited to twelve weeks of treatment, which makes the twelve-week mark the default deprescribing trigger.

sources.label: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Dementia

subtopic_detail: Managing a narrow therapeutic index drug when renal function falls acutely
stem:
An 83-year-old woman presents with a week of nausea, poor appetite and lethargy. She has permanent atrial fibrillation treated with digoxin 250 micrograms daily and apixaban 5 mg twice daily, and takes indapamide for hypertension.

She had four days of loose stools a fortnight ago after a family barbecue and has been drinking little since. She has not vomited and has no abdominal pain.

She is alert and orientated, her capillary refill is three seconds, and her blood pressure does not fall on standing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 52/min irregularly irregular, blood pressure 118/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Digoxin 3.1 nmol/L (0.5-2.0), creatinine 168 micromol/L (45-90, was 92 six weeks ago), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular response and no ectopy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Withhold digoxin, correct the potassium and magnesium, and repeat the level tomorrow
options.rationale: Chronic digoxin toxicity without arrhythmia or haemodynamic compromise is managed by withholding the drug, correcting the electrolyte disturbances that potentiate it, restoring volume and monitoring; hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia both increase digoxin binding at the sodium-potassium pump. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Give digoxin-specific antibody fragments and admit her for continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Antibody fragments are reserved for life-threatening arrhythmia, haemodynamic instability or hyperkalaemia above 5.0 mmol/L in acute poisoning, none of which is present with a stable rate of 52 and a low potassium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Wilderness)

options.text: Halve the digoxin dose, replace potassium orally, and repeat the level weekly
options.rationale: Continuing any digoxin while the level is above the therapeutic range and creatinine is still rising allows further accumulation, and a week is too long an interval for reassessment. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue digoxin, give intravenous fluid, and repeat renal function in 24 hours
options.rationale: Rehydration is necessary but continuing the causative drug through an episode of acute kidney injury keeps the level supratherapeutic. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Insert a temporary pacing wire and withhold digoxin until the ventricular rate rises
options.rationale: Temporary pacing is for symptomatic or haemodynamically significant bradycardia, and a rate of 52 in an alert, normotensive patient does not qualify. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Digoxin is almost entirely renally cleared with a narrow therapeutic index, so any fall in glomerular filtration converts a stable dose into a toxic one. In older people the presentation is insidious and non-specific: anorexia, nausea, fatigue, confusion and visual disturbance, often attributed to ageing or to the illness that caused the dehydration. Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, frequently from a thiazide-like diuretic, both amplify digoxin binding to the sodium-potassium ATPase and make toxicity occur at lower serum concentrations. Chronic toxicity is usually managed conservatively, and after recovery the question is whether digoxin is needed at all, since it is no longer a first-line rate-control agent. In context, a narrow therapeutic index drug should be reviewed whenever an older person becomes acutely unwell, because the illness itself changes the clearance.
key_points: Any acute kidney injury converts a stable digoxin dose into a toxic one
Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia potentiate digoxin at any given level
Chronic toxicity without arrhythmia or instability is managed by withholding and correcting electrolytes
Antibody fragments are reserved for arrhythmia, instability or hyperkalaemia in acute poisoning
explanation.pearls: Serum potassium above 5.0 mmol/L in acute digoxin poisoning is itself an indication for digoxin-specific antibody fragments, because it reflects the degree of sodium-potassium ATPase blockade rather than total body potassium.

subtopic_detail: Movement disorder emerging after a recently started antiemetic
stem:
A 78-year-old man is brought in by his wife because he has slowed down over the past three months. He shuffles when he walks, has stopped playing the piano and takes twice as long to dress.

Four months ago he was started on metoclopramide for nausea after an admission with gastritis, and it has been continued since.

On examination there is bradykinesia with equal decrement in finger tapping on both sides and a symmetrical rest tremor of both hands. His wife confirms that his sense of smell is unchanged and that he has never acted out his dreams. His handwriting is smaller than it was a year ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 138/80 mmHg supine and 132/78 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Medications: Metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily, pantoprazole 20 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start levodopa with carbidopa 100/25 mg three times daily and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Starting dopaminergic therapy while a dopamine antagonist continues treats the effect of a drug with another drug, and a partial response would muddy the diagnosis further. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange a dopamine transporter scan before making any change to his current medicines
options.rationale: Functional imaging can separate drug-induced from degenerative parkinsonism, but it is expensive, not first-line, and unnecessary when a simple therapeutic withdrawal will answer the question. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Cease the metoclopramide and reassess his movements over the next three months
options.rationale: Symmetrical bradykinesia and rest tremor beginning within months of a dopamine antagonist, with preserved olfaction and no dream enactment, fits drug-induced parkinsonism; withdrawal is both the treatment and the diagnostic test, though recovery can take three to six months. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Start amantadine 100 mg twice daily and continue metoclopramide for his nausea
options.rationale: Amantadine gives modest symptomatic relief but leaving the causative antagonist in place guarantees the problem persists, and amantadine adds confusion and livedo reticularis in older people. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Add benztropine 1 mg twice daily and refer him to neurology for further assessment
options.rationale: Anticholinergics may help drug-induced tremor but cause confusion, constipation and urinary retention in older people, and adding a drug to counter a drug is a prescribing cascade. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Polypharmacy)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Polypharmacy

explanation.summary: Drug-induced parkinsonism is the second most common cause of parkinsonism in older people and is routinely mislabelled as idiopathic disease, which leads to years of unnecessary dopaminergic therapy. The usual culprits are the typical and atypical antipsychotics, metoclopramide and prochlorperazine, all dopamine D2 antagonists, and less commonly sodium valproate, lithium and some calcium channel blockers. Features favouring a drug cause are symmetry, a temporal relationship to the drug, prominent postural tremor, and the absence of the pre-motor features of idiopathic disease such as hyposmia, constipation and rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder. Australian labelling restricts metoclopramide to short courses of up to five days for this reason. In context, a new movement disorder in an older person is a medication review before it is a neurology referral.
key_points: Metoclopramide and prochlorperazine are common and reversible causes of parkinsonism
Symmetry and preserved olfaction favour a drug cause over idiopathic disease
Withdrawal is both the treatment and the diagnostic test
Improvement may take three to six months, and some patients unmask underlying disease
explanation.pearls: Australian product information restricts metoclopramide to a maximum of five days of treatment because of the risk of extrapyramidal adverse effects, which are most likely in people over 65 and in those under 20.

sources.label: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Polypharmacy

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation decision in a recurrent faller with atrial fibrillation
stem:
An 86-year-old woman with permanent atrial fibrillation, hypertension and type 2 diabetes is reviewed after her third fall in six months. Each fall happened outdoors on uneven footpaths while she was wearing backless slippers, and none caused a fracture or a head strike.

A locum has written in her notes that her apixaban should be stopped because she keeps falling. Her daughter agrees and asks you to sign the cessation.

She weighs 68 kg and has had no bleeding episode since apixaban was started three years ago. Her blood pressure is recorded supine and again at three minutes standing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min irregularly irregular, blood pressure 148/82 mmHg supine and 124/74 mmHg standing at three minutes, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-165), platelets 244 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 96 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 48 mL/min/1.73m2
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily, perindopril 10 mg daily, indapamide 1.5 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her anticoagulation?

options.text: Stop apixaban and start aspirin 100 mg daily to reduce her overall bleeding risk
options.rationale: Aspirin provides minimal stroke protection in atrial fibrillation while retaining a bleeding risk close to that of anticoagulation, so this trades away benefit without removing harm. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Australian clinical guidelines for the diagnosis and management of atrial fibrillation)
source_refs: NHFA/CSANZ Australian clinical guidelines for the diagnosis and management of atrial fibrillation

options.text: Continue apixaban at full dose and address her modifiable falls risk factors
options.rationale: Falls risk alone is not a reason to withhold anticoagulation, since modelling suggests a patient would need to fall hundreds of times a year for the bleeding risk to outweigh stroke prevention; she also meets only one of the three dose-reduction criteria, so the full dose stands while the orthostatic drop, footwear and footpath hazards are addressed. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Australian clinical guidelines for the diagnosis and management of atrial fibrillation)
source_refs: NHFA/CSANZ Australian clinical guidelines for the diagnosis and management of atrial fibrillation

options.text: Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily given her age and her recurrent falls
options.rationale: The reduced dose requires two of age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, and creatinine 133 micromol/L or more; she meets age only, and under-dosing a direct oral anticoagulant is associated with higher stroke rates without lower bleeding. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Stop apixaban and refer her for percutaneous left atrial appendage closure instead
options.rationale: Device closure is reserved for patients with an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation, such as recurrent major bleeding, and carries its own procedural risk plus a period of antithrombotic therapy afterwards. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Australian clinical guidelines for the diagnosis and management of atrial fibrillation)
source_refs: NHFA/CSANZ Australian clinical guidelines for the diagnosis and management of atrial fibrillation

options.text: Stop apixaban for three months while she completes a falls prevention programme
options.rationale: A three-month interruption exposes her to an unmitigated stroke risk during exactly the period her fall risk is being reduced, and interruptions frequently become permanent. (Source: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls)
source_refs: RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls

explanation.summary: Withholding anticoagulation because an older patient falls is one of the most common and most costly errors in geriatric prescribing, because the stroke prevented is usually far more disabling than the bleed feared. Modelling from the warfarin era suggested a patient would need to fall on the order of 300 times a year for the intracranial haemorrhage risk to outweigh the stroke reduction, and the direct oral anticoagulants carry roughly half the intracranial bleeding risk of warfarin. The correct response to a faller on anticoagulation is to keep the anticoagulant and attack the falls: postural blood pressure, sedating and hypotensive medicines, footwear, vision, and a supervised strength and balance programme. Inappropriate dose reduction of a direct oral anticoagulant is a separate and frequent error that raises stroke risk without lowering bleeding. In context, the intuitive response to a visible risk can cause more harm than the invisible risk it is meant to avoid, which is why the decision belongs to the numbers rather than to the anecdote.
key_points: Falls risk alone does not justify withholding anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation
Aspirin is not a safer substitute for an anticoagulant in atrial fibrillation
Apixaban dose reduction requires two of age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or more
The response to a faller on anticoagulation is to treat the falls
explanation.pearls: An orthostatic systolic drop of 20 mmHg or more at three minutes is itself the most treatable falls risk factor in a patient on multiple antihypertensives, and here it points to the indapamide and perindopril rather than the apixaban.

sources.label: NHFA/CSANZ Australian clinical guidelines for the diagnosis and management of atrial fibrillation
RACGP Aged Care Clinical Guide (Silver Book) - Falls

subtopic_detail: Converting oral oxycodone to a subcutaneous morphine infusion when the oral route is lost
stem:
A 72-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer is being cared for at home. For the past week his pain has been well controlled on his current oral opioid regimen, and he has needed only one breakthrough dose in the last 48 hours.

Since yesterday he has vomited every oral dose within minutes and has kept nothing down. He remains alert and comfortable at rest, with no myoclonus and pupils of 3 mm.

His renal and liver function are unchanged from a month ago. A continuous subcutaneous infusion is to be started this afternoon.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 74 micromol/L (60-110), estimated glomerular filtration rate >60 mL/min/1.73m2, liver function tests within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Slow-release oxycodone 30 mg twice daily, immediate-release oxycodone 5 mg as required, macrogol daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate 24-hour subcutaneous morphine regimen to commence?

options.text: Morphine 15 mg over 24 hours, with morphine 2.5 mg subcutaneously hourly as required
options.rationale: This applies both the more conservative 3 to 1 oral-to-subcutaneous ratio and a further cross-tolerance reduction, double-discounting a dose in a patient whose pain is currently controlled and risking withdrawal and breakthrough pain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Morphine 60 mg over 24 hours, with morphine 10 mg subcutaneously hourly as required
options.rationale: This transfers the oral oxycodone dose milligram for milligram to subcutaneous morphine, applying neither the drug conversion nor the route conversion, and delivers roughly four times the intended dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic)

options.text: Morphine 45 mg over 24 hours, with morphine 7.5 mg subcutaneously hourly as required
options.rationale: The drug and route conversions are correct but no allowance has been made for incomplete cross-tolerance, which is the standard safety margin when the opioid itself is changed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Morphine 30 mg over 24 hours, with morphine 5 mg subcutaneously hourly as required
options.rationale: Oral oxycodone 60 mg is about 90 mg of oral morphine, which halves to 45 mg by the subcutaneous route, and a one third reduction for incomplete cross-tolerance gives 30 mg over 24 hours with a breakthrough dose of one sixth, or 5 mg; the reduction also absorbs the uncertainty between the 2 to 1 and 3 to 1 oral-to-subcutaneous ratios in use. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

options.text: Morphine 90 mg over 24 hours, with morphine 15 mg subcutaneously hourly as required
options.rationale: This is the oral morphine equivalent dose given by the subcutaneous route, omitting the route conversion entirely and delivering about three times the intended dose. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Opioid conversion errors are among the most frequent serious prescribing errors in palliative care, and they cluster around two omissions: forgetting that the parenteral route needs a smaller dose, and forgetting the reduction for incomplete cross-tolerance when the drug is changed. Published conversion ratios vary between sources, with oral to subcutaneous morphine quoted as anywhere from 2 to 1 to 3 to 1, which is precisely why a 25 to 33 per cent reduction is applied and the patient is reviewed within 24 hours rather than the ratio being treated as exact. The reduction is omitted only when pain is uncontrolled, when the deficit is made up through the breakthrough dose instead. Breakthrough dosing is conventionally one sixth of the 24-hour dose by the same route, available hourly, and repeated requirement for it is the signal to increase the infusion. In context, published conversion ratios are approximations, and the safety of a rotation comes from the reduction and the early review rather than from the arithmetic being exact.
key_points: Oral oxycodone to oral morphine is approximately 1 to 1.5
Oral morphine to subcutaneous morphine is approximately 2 to 1
Reduce by 25 to 33 per cent for incomplete cross-tolerance when changing opioid
Breakthrough dose is one sixth of the 24-hour dose by the same route
explanation.pearls: Count the breakthrough doses used in the previous 24 hours and add that total to the next infusion: three 5 mg breakthroughs on a 30 mg infusion means the next 24-hour dose is 45 mg.

subtopic_detail: Agitated delirium in hospital when the admission medication history is incomplete
stem:
A 79-year-old woman is on day 3 of admission after a fall that fractured her left pubic ramus. Overnight she became agitated and tremulous, has not slept for two nights, and tells the nurses there are small animals moving along the curtain rail.

She is drenched in sweat despite being afebrile. There is a fine postural tremor of both outstretched hands. Her chest is clear, her abdomen is soft, and a bladder scan shows a residual of 40 mL. She drinks one glass of wine at Christmas and her breath alcohol on admission was zero.

Her general practitioner's list, faxed this morning, includes diazepam 10 mg nightly prescribed for the past twenty years, which was not charted on admission. She is orientated to person but not to place, and her attention fluctuates through the day.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 158/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 7.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 6 mg/L (<5), sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 82 micromol/L (45-90), corrected calcium 2.36 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), urine dipstick positive for nitrites and leukocyte esterase

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral haloperidol 0.5 mg twice daily and continue it until her agitation settles
options.rationale: An antipsychotic suppresses the agitation without treating the withdrawal driving it, lowers the seizure threshold at the point of highest seizure risk, and adds extrapyramidal and cardiac risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start oral trimethoprim 300 mg at night and repeat the urine culture later
options.rationale: A positive dipstick in an afebrile older woman with a normal white cell count, a C-reactive protein of 6 and no urinary symptoms indicates asymptomatic bacteriuria, which is present in up to half of hospitalised older women and should not be treated. (Source: ACSQHC Antimicrobial Stewardship Clinical Care Standard)
source_refs: ACSQHC Antimicrobial Stewardship Clinical Care Standard

options.text: Arrange a non-contrast CT brain and an electroencephalogram before starting any treatment
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is indicated for focal signs, head injury or unexplained failure to improve, and delaying treatment for an electroencephalogram in an identified withdrawal syndrome risks a seizure while she waits. (Source: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people)
source_refs: ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people

options.text: Start olanzapine 2.5 mg at night and nurse her in a low-stimulus single room
options.rationale: Environmental measures are appropriate adjuncts but an antipsychotic is the wrong pharmacological class here; sedative withdrawal is the one delirium in which a benzodiazepine is the treatment rather than a precipitant. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Chart diazepam at her usual dose and plan a slow dose reduction after discharge
options.rationale: Autonomic arousal, tremor, insomnia and visual hallucinations beginning around 72 hours after an unintended cessation, with normal inflammatory markers and no alcohol history, is benzodiazepine withdrawal; reinstating her established dose stops the syndrome and prevents withdrawal seizures, with any reduction deferred to a supervised taper over months once she is well. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Unintended cessation of a long-term benzodiazepine at the point of hospital admission is a preventable cause of agitated delirium, and it is missed because the drug is rarely volunteered by the patient and often absent from the referral letter. Diazepam has a long half-life with active metabolites, so withdrawal characteristically declares itself two to seven days after the last dose rather than within hours, by which time the admission is usually attributed to something else. The clinical picture is sympathetic overactivity with tremor, sweating, insomnia and perceptual disturbance, and the danger is a withdrawal seizure. Medication reconciliation within 24 hours of admission is the systems-level fix, and the positive urine dipstick in this scenario is the classic distractor, since asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in hospitalised older women and treating it neither helps the delirium nor prevents harm. In context, an accurate admission medication history prevents more delirium than any drug treats.
key_points: Long half-life benzodiazepine withdrawal presents two to seven days after the last dose
Autonomic arousal with tremor, sweating and hallucinations distinguishes it from other delirium
Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and do not treat the withdrawal
Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in hospitalised older women and is not treated
explanation.pearls: Reinstating the patient's usual benzodiazepine dose settles a withdrawal delirium within hours, and any dose reduction is then a supervised outpatient taper of 10 to 25 per cent every one to two weeks rather than an inpatient project.

ANZSGM position statement on delirium in older people
